stories.headline: NASDAQ NOTCHES FRESH RECORD AS SLIDING OIL OFFSETS HAWKISH FED CHATTER, S&P FLAT
stories.body: The Nasdaq 100 rose 0.59% to 30,662 for a second straight record close while the S&P 500 was essentially flat at 7,761 (-0.05%) and the Dow slipped about 0.3%, as falling oil prices gave growth stocks room to run even as fresh hawkish comments from Fed officials kept the broader tape in check.
stories.explain: The divergence between the Nasdaq's record and the S&P's flat print comes down to duration: mega-cap tech names are long-duration assets whose valuations are most sensitive to the future cost of capital, so falling energy input costs and a softer inflation trajectory disproportionately lift their present value even on a day when hawkish Fedspeak is nudging the broader rate outlook higher. The S&P, weighted more toward cyclicals and financials that benefit less from that specific dynamic, ends up pinned near unchanged as the two forces roughly cancel out.

stories.headline: WTI SLIDES TO ~$90, BRENT HOLDS NEAR $100 IN FOURTH-PLUS SESSION OF IRAN-DRIVEN LOSSES
stories.body: WTI crude fell roughly 2.3% to around $90 a barrel and Brent held near $100, extending a losing streak that began when diplomatic progress on Iran started unwinding the war-risk premium priced into crude, with tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz continuing to move without disruption.
stories.explain: Oil prices embed a probability-weighted risk premium for supply disruption whenever a major producer faces conflict risk, separate from the price justified by actual current supply and demand. As diplomatic talks credibly lower the odds of a Hormuz disruption, that premium bleeds out of the price day by day even though no barrels have actually stopped flowing, which is exactly the mechanical reason WTI keeps grinding lower in a fourth-plus straight session rather than moving in one sharp repricing.

stories.headline: TREASURY YIELDS LITTLE CHANGED AT 4.96% AS TRADERS AWAIT MORE FED CLUES
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield was roughly flat at 4.96% (-1 bp) and the 2-year eased to about 4.74%, as investors held positioning steady heading into a week of additional Fed commentary following last Wednesday's 25-bp hike to 3.75%-4.00%.
stories.explain: The 10-year yield reflects the market's expected average path of short-term rates plus a term premium, so when the calendar is full of scheduled Fed speakers but no new data has landed yet, yields tend to sit still rather than move on rumor — traders are waiting for actual signal before repricing the expected hike path further. That's a different dynamic from a data-driven move: it's the market explicitly pausing to listen rather than reacting to a concrete catalyst.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS TO ~$4,308 IN SECOND STRAIGHT LOSING SESSION AS DOLLAR FIRMS, FED TALK TURNS HAWKISH
stories.body: Gold fell about 0.8% to roughly $4,308 an ounce, its second consecutive down session, as a firmer dollar (DXY +0.3% to 100.65) and hawkish commentary from Fed officials pulled speculative capital out of the metals complex even with gold still near record territory for the year.
stories.explain: Gold is priced in dollars and competes with real (inflation-adjusted) yields as a store of value, so it faces a double headwind when the dollar strengthens and officials talk up the odds of tighter policy: a stronger dollar makes gold costlier for foreign buyers, while hawkish rhetoric that lifts the expected real-rate path raises the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset. Both channels are working in the same direction today, which is why gold is giving back ground even though nothing in the underlying inflation picture has actually changed since Friday.

stories.headline: TRUMP-XI SUMMIT THIS WEEK PUTS AI, TARIFFS AND CRITICAL MINERALS BACK IN FOCUS
stories.body: A high-profile meeting between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping is set for later this week, with AI export controls, tariff levels and critical-minerals supply chains all on the agenda — a swing factor markets are watching alongside the Fed for the next directional catalyst.
stories.explain: Trade-policy headlines move markets through the same discounted-cash-flow channel as Fed policy, but on the input-cost and market-access side rather than the discount-rate side: a tariff or export-control change directly alters the future earnings multinationals can expect to generate in China and vice versa, so the market prices in a probability-weighted range of summit outcomes ahead of time and then re-rates sharply on the actual announcement, much like it does around FOMC decisions.

stories.headline: TEXAS TECH, NEBRASKA LAND MARQUEE 2026 COMMITS AS TENNESSEE'S RALPH SCOTT FACES SEASON-ENDING KNEE SURGERY
stories.body: Four-star point guard Aaron Britt Jr. committed to Grant McCasland's Texas Tech as the program's first pledge of the cycle, Fred Hoiberg landed the highest-ranked recruit in Nebraska history in four-star forward Dawson Battie, and Tennessee freshman Ralph Scott is set for knee surgery that will sideline him at least six months.

stories.headline: PISTONS BUMP JALEN DUREN OFFER TO $200M AS BUCKS EMERGE AS NEW SUITOR, NO DEAL AT MEDIA DAYS' OPENING
stories.body: Detroit has raised its extension offer to Jalen Duren to five years, $200 million — up from $190 million — but the All-NBA center is still holding out for closer to his Rose Rule max of $287 million, with the Milwaukee Bucks now reportedly joining Sacramento as a possible trade suitor as the Rockets and Mavericks kick off 2026-27 Media Days with camp about a week away.

stories.headline: BEARS' QB ROOM DEPLETES AS CALEB WILLIAMS, TYSON BAGENT BOTH UNCERTAIN FOR MONDAY VS. EAGLES
stories.body: Chicago could turn to Case Keenum against Philadelphia on Monday night with Caleb Williams (hamstring) and Tyson Bagent (concussion) both in question, while Atlanta confirmed Michael Penix Jr. starts Week 3 versus Green Bay and the Rams' Matthew Stafford threw four touchdowns, two to Davante Adams, in a Monday-night rout of the Giants.

stories.headline: TEXAS TECH DOUBLES DOWN ON TRANSFER SPENDING AFTER BIG 12 TITLE AS MIAMI'S $10M MENSAH BET HEADLINES PORTAL ARMS RACE
stories.body: Fresh off winning the Big 12 and reaching the CFP semifinal, Texas Tech has assembled another elite transfer class to defend its title, part of a broader spending arms race that includes Miami's reported $10 million NIL deal for transfer quarterback Darian Mensah, the portal's top-ranked signal-caller this cycle.

deepDive.title: Forward Guidance: How the Fed Moves Markets Without Touching Rates
content: Today's tape has an odd feature: the Fed took no action, yet Treasury yields, the dollar, and gold all moved on "hawkish commentary" from Fed officials alone. The 10-year sat at 4.96 percent, little changed, explicitly because traders were awaiting more Fed clues rather than reacting to data. That's forward guidance doing its job — the idea that a central bank can shift financial conditions through words and signals about the future path of policy, not just through the rate decisions it actually votes on. It matters today because it's the same mechanism knitting together three separate stories in this brief: flat yields, a firmer dollar, and softer gold.

The mechanism runs through market-implied rate expectations. When a Fed official gives a speech that leans hawkish — emphasizing sticky inflation risk over labor-market softness, for instance — traders immediately reprice fed funds futures and SOFR futures to reflect a higher probability of another hike or a longer hold at restrictive levels. That repriced path feeds straight into the dollar (wider expected rate differentials support DXY, which is why it firmed 0.3 percent to 100.65 today) and into gold (a higher expected real-rate path raises the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset, which is why gold fell for a second straight session). None of this requires an actual FOMC vote; it only requires the market to believe the signal.

What's easy to miss is how much more efficient this channel became once central banks started deliberately using it as policy. Ben Bernanke's 2013 "taper tantrum" is the canonical example in reverse: he merely mentioned slowing bond purchases in congressional testimony, no purchases were actually reduced yet, and the 10-year yield still jumped roughly 100 basis points over the following two months as markets repriced the entire expected path of policy off a single sentence. That episode taught the Fed that words can move long-term borrowing costs as much as, or more than, actual balance-sheet or rate changes — which is exactly why a calendar full of scheduled Fed speakers, with no new data due, can hold today's market in a defensive crouch.

The read-through for the rest of this week is that markets are trading news of upcoming speeches as much as the speeches themselves. With last Wednesday's 25-bp hike to 3.75%-4.00% still fresh and officials now testing how hawkish they can sound without triggering a bigger repricing, watch whether the 10-year holds near 4.96 percent or breaks meaningfully higher on any given day's Fedspeak — that move, more than the WTI slide or the Trump-Xi summit headlines, is the cleanest real-time read on how much more tightening the market now expects the Fed to deliver.
